figures.alt_text: A timeline of 12 sensor sites through the 2026-10-10 data cutoff. Coverage is uneven: the longest records run from 2026-03-03, while the shortest Loudoun County record begins on 2026-06-18 and the 3 sites outside Loudoun County begin in September 2026. All 6 sensors in the common window were collecting together only from 2026-06-18 to 2026-08-07.
figures.caption: The shaded band is the window in which all 6 sensors were collecting; the darker band is the wildfire smoke transport weekend, which DEQ's IF qualifier identifies; whether it is an exceptional event is a determination for the US EPA and is unresolved. Dotted lines mark the end of the regulatory monitor record and the network reconfiguration.

The site with the shortest record, DC-06 at 51 days, carries the highest own-record value; DC-01 has 152 days. On the common window 5 of 6 sites sit above the 35 microgram line; with the smoke window excluded, none do, the values running from 16.644 to 24.356.
figures.caption: Own-record against common-window 98th percentiles, with record days annotated. A 98th percentile read from a 51-day record is a different order statistic from one read from 152 days. Triangles give the common-window value with every day from 2026-07-16 to 2026-07-19 excluded, local standard time days; the own-record values with that window excluded are in the own-record table. The horizontal line marks the level of the 24-hour standard and is not a threshold being crossed: neither these values nor DEQ's are comparable to the NAAQS.

figures.alt_text: A 6-by-6 matrix of pairwise correlations, every cell labelled. All 15 pairs fall between 0.886 and 0.966, so the sensors largely rise and fall together across the network.
figures.caption: Pearson correlation of hourly PM2.5 between each pair of sensors, pairwise-complete, smoke window excluded, exact zeros treated as missing. With the smoke window included the pairs fall between 0.959 and 0.991 (the data table gives each pair both ways). Descriptive only: high spatial correlation does not establish that local sources contribute nothing, since the network may sit largely upwind and a local increment can be masked by a dominant regional signal.

figures.alt_text: Two separate horizontal stacked bars. The upper bar shows that 88.61 percent of asthma GWAS discovery individuals sit in the European category. The lower bar shows Loudoun County residents by self-identified race, a different measurement of a different population.
figures.caption: Upper panel: initial-stage discovery individuals across the asthma studies in GWAS Catalog release 2026-11-02, by the catalogue's broad ancestral category. Lower panel: Loudoun County residents by self-identified race, ACS 2024 5-year estimates (acs/acs5), table B02001. ACS categories are self-identified race and ethnicity, which are social categories and not genetic ancestry. They are shown only to describe the population the atlas is meant to serve. The two panels have separate axes and are not comparable: one counts people enrolled in studies and groups them by genetic ancestry, the other counts residents and groups them by a social category.
figures.limitation: Descriptive only, and not an effect estimate: these are study sample sizes and resident counts, and v1 computes no cross-ancestry gene-environment effect. The discovery composition is the composition of the published evidence base, not of any population: a category with few individuals means the evidence was measured in few people from it, which is a property of who was studied and not of anyone's genome. Because the asthma evidence base is predominantly European, every locus count here rests mostly on European-ancestry discovery samples, and findings from that base transfer unevenly to other groups. A study sample naming several broad ancestral categories is split equally across them, because the catalogue publishes no per-category count within a row. The discovery total is a sum of study sample sizes and not a headcount: asthma studies draw repeatedly on the same cohorts, so a participant in several studies is counted once per study.
